abstract: As a functional nucleic acid motif is optimized, better variants become less abundant in sequence space and significantly more difficult to identify. Here, we used two types of libraries to discover an improved variant of a previously optimized light-producing deoxyribozyme called Supernova. One library was designed in such a way that most mutations were consistent with the sequence requirements and secondary structure of this catalytic motif. The second contained short stretches of random sequence in place of AAAA spacers previously introduced in minimization experiments. Catalytically active sequences were isolated from each library using single and multiple round selections. Mutations from the best deoxyribozymes were then combined to yield an improved variant containing 12 mutations, which we named Hypernova. The rate of Hypernova at subsaturating substrate concentrations was up to 97-fold higher than that of Supernova, and its initial rate of light production was up to 30-fold faster. In addition, sensors constructed using Hypernova outperformed those made from Supernova in three different assays. These results indicate that Hypernova can enhance the performance of light-producing deoxyribozyme sensors for applications such as diagnostics and high-throughput screening.
